core: Human-environment interaction: people adapt to, modify, and depend on the natural environment (a two-way relationship)
Environmental determinism as a historical, now-discredited idea, including its misuse to justify racism and colonialism
Possibilism as the mainstream successor: the environment sets limits and offers possibilities among which humans choose
Natural resources: renewable vs non-renewable, and the idea of sustainability
The ecological footprint concept (demand on nature vs biocapacity)
Political ecology in one sentence: environmental problems are shaped by power and economy, not only by nature
supporting: Brundtland/EPA framing of sustainability as meeting present and future needs
Earth Overshoot Day and the '1.7 Earths' framing as an illustration of overshoot

Agricultural systems and food production detail (owned by agriculture)

claims.claim: The human-environment relationship is two-way: the environment shapes human activity and humans in turn shape and change Earth's surface and atmosphere.
Environmental determinism is the idea that the natural or physical environment shapes and essentially dictates culture; it has been largely rejected by modern geographers.

Environmental determinism carried racist undertones: in the 1920s determinists claimed tropical peoples were 'slothful and backward' while Europeans in 'stimulating' climates were more industrious, a framing used to justify colonial and racial hierarchies.
Possibilism holds that people can adapt to their environmental conditions and choose from many alternatives (possibilities) despite the limits the environment poses.

The Ecological Footprint measures human demand on nature and compares it with biocapacity (the productivity of ecological assets), expressed in global hectares of world-average productivity; it was conceived in 1990 by Mathis Wackernagel and William Rees.

Humanity is currently using nature about 1.7 times faster than Earth's ecosystems can regenerate, equivalent to using about 1.7 Earths; the point in the year when annual demand exceeds annual regeneration is Earth Overshoot Day.
EPA defines sustainability as creating and maintaining conditions under which humans and nature can exist in productive harmony to support present and future generations.
Political ecology studies how political-economic power relations shape environmental change and who wins or loses from it, arguing many environmental problems are as much social as ecological.
A country whose Ecological Footprint exceeds its biocapacity runs an ecological deficit; over 80 percent of the world's population lives in countries running such deficits.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact date of Earth Overshoot Day and the precise 'number of Earths' figure move slightly year to year as Global Footprint Network recalculates all years with the latest data.
positions: Recent Earth Overshoot Day dates have fallen in late July (e.g., July 24 in 2025 per the Overshoot Day site).
The headline framing '1.7 Earths' / 'using nature 1.7 times faster than it regenerates' is Global Footprint Network's durable summary figure.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Lesson uses the durable '~1.7 Earths' framing attributed to Global Footprint Network and describes Earth Overshoot Day conceptually (late July in recent years) rather than pinning a single fragile date.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Human Geography (University System of Georgia) - 1.8 The Human-Environment Relationship; 1.9 Key Terms; Ch. 13 Environment and Resources
sourceRecords.provider: University System of Georgia (Dorrell & Henderson), via WSU Pressbooks
sourceRecords.notes: Open human-geography textbook (CC BY 4.0, © 2019 University System of Georgia). Chapter 1.8 defines the human-environment relationship, environmental determinism ('largely rejected', with explicit note of its racist undertones and the 1920s tropical-vs-temperate framing) and names possibilism; chapter 1.9 key terms give the possibilism definition (people can adapt and choose from many possibilities despite environmental limits); chapter 13 covers renewable vs non-renewable resources. Facts verified against the source; all lesson prose original, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Ecological Footprint (overview)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary organization behind the Ecological Footprint metric. Supports: the footprint measures demand on nature vs biocapacity; biocapacity is the productivity of cropland, grazing land, forest, fishing grounds, and built-up land; the global hectare is a hectare of world-average productivity; the concept was conceived in 1990 by Mathis Wackernagel and William Rees at UBC; over 80% of the world's population lives in countries running ecological deficits. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: About Earth Overshoot Day
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the definition of Earth Overshoot Day (the date each year when humanity's demand for ecological resources exceeds what Earth can regenerate that year) and the durable '~1.7 Earths / 1.7 times faster than regeneration' framing. Notes that all years since 1961 are recalculated annually, so the exact date shifts; recent dates fall in late July (July 24 in 2025 per the site). No wording reproduced.
